figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Paper-to-result reproduction in computational quantum science. a, Scientific papers from three research directions in computational quantum science are converted into reproduction tasks centred on a target figure within OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment. In OmniQ, a plan agent and an execute agent reproduce the source code and the target figure, and a judge agent compares the reproduced figure with the published one. b, The mechanism of the self-improving AI scientist RA for computational quantum science. The planner decomposes a research plan into sub-plans, each executed by an executor and evaluated by a critic. Failed steps are revised and re-executed, with the planner replanning when necessary. A judge evaluates the assembled result. Upon failure, expert feedback is processed by the residual agent to refine executor guidance, critic criteria and planner strategies.
figures.headline: The schematic shows OmniQ converting papers into reproduction tasks and RA revising failed steps through a planner, executor and critic.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 1a, OmniQ is employed to curate 60 studies spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization.
As shown in Fig. 1b, RA splits a reproduction task into sub-plans and coordinates three roles powered by the same base LLM.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: AI-assisted reproduction reveals inconsistencies in the scientific record. a, Reproduction assessment across three directions of computational quantum science. Grey denotes studies with no identified problem, whereas increasingly dark red indicates Level I–III issues according to their severity and resolvability. b–d, Representative Level I–III cases. From top to bottom, each case shows the scientific problem, the identified reproduction issue—including the paper’s claim, the contradiction found by the AI scientist and expert feedback—and the reproduced results before and after expert correction, each compared with the original result. For the panel b, a machine-learning configuration discrepancy resolved using the released code. For the panel c, an ambiguous experimental procedure requiring expert resolution. For the panel d, a fundamental inconsistency between the reported quantity, released code and theoretical constraints that cannot be resolved from the available scientific record. Dashed black and solid red curves denote the reported and reproduced results, respectively.
figures.headline: Reproduction assessment flags 18 of 60 studies, with Level I to III issues ranging from missing details to unresolvable contradictions.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 2a, this procedure identifies reproducibility issues in 18 of the 60 studies.
As shown in the third panel of Fig. 2b, following the written description causes the reproduced model to lose its reported advantage in the extrapolation regime.

As shown in the third panel of Fig. 2c, the silhouette coefficient, which measures clustering quality from $-1$ (poor) to $1$ (well separated), decreases from approximately $0.59$ in the paper to $0.29$ in the reproduction at circuit depth four.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Performance of RA for computational quantum science. Reproduction success across 59 reproduction tasks is plotted against model-inference cost per task on a logarithmic scale. Marker shape denotes the agent system or harness type, marker color denotes the underlying model family or access mode, and marker size indicates wall-clock time per task; semi-transparent markers denote earlier model generations. Labels identify the corresponding model or harness. RA, the proposed self-improving AI scientist, runs DSH as its executor and is drawn as the DSH marker inside a gear; the dashed line indicates the Pareto frontier between reproduction success and inference cost. A brown ring marks GPT models accessed through an application programming interface (API).
figures.headline: Plotting success against inference cost shows RA matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at about a third of its cost.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 summarizes reproduction success together with inference cost per task and wall-clock time across different agents and harness mechanisms.
As shown in Fig. 3, Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5, Kimi Code with K3, and several Codex-based systems use larger inference budgets than Claude Code with Opus 5.5 yet perform worse.

As illustrated in Fig. 3, third-party harnesses span a wide performance range, from about $19\%$ for Meta-Harness with DeepSeek to $48\%$ for mini-swe-agent with DeepSeek, all substantially below the strongest first-party systems.

abstract:
AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated. These results establish a new paradigm for computational quantum research, where published results become reusable scientific capabilities that support autonomous discovery.

Project page: https://omniq-qid-lab.github.io/

sections.body: The introduction frames computational quantum science around three areas: classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization. It states that prior AI-driven discovery in the field is fragmented and confined to narrow settings. The authors propose OmniQ, which turns a full paper and a target result into a reproduction task. The agent rebuilds the method, runs it under a comparable computational budget and attempts to match the reported outcome. Expert intervention is reserved for ambiguous or inconsistent cases. Using OmniQ, the authors evaluate five LLM-powered AI scientists and six third-party agent harnesses across 60 papers. In 18 studies, the paper description, released code and reported results are inconsistent, which the authors say makes it hard to separate agent failure from limits of the scientific record.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Computational quantum science needs autonomous discovery, and paper-to-result reproduction is proposed as its verifiable starting point.

sections.body:
The section defines three reproduction levels and illustrates each with one case. Level III, Paper #60, was excluded, leaving 59 papers. Across systems, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 reaches about 93% success, Codex with GPT-6-luna about 42%, and Meta-Harness with DeepSeek 19%. Success does not rise monotonically with inference cost. Third-party harnesses range from about 19% to 48%, all below the first-party systems.

Residual Agents (RA) uses a planner, executors and a critic, with a residual memory of verified repairs. A human expert reviews each proposed update. On 59 tasks, with five used for development and 54 unseen, RA lifts DeepSeek V4.1 Flash from 68% to about 85% at USD 5.6 per task. The authors note that the best system still scores higher, and that 90% of successful tasks needed at least one correction.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Frontier agents reproduce up to about 93% of tasks, and a self-improving agent lifts a weaker model from 68% to 85%.

sections.body:
The discussion states that reliable reproduction depends jointly on agent capability and on the consistency of the scientific record. It describes RA as converting verified reproduction failures into reusable experience without modifying the underlying model. The verified workflows are made available through an extensible research platform.

The authors name three future directions. The first is extending OmniQ to fully autonomous reproduction across disciplines, citing related work in biology, machine learning and social sciences. The second is improving performance, through adaptive test-time computation, specialized tools and adaptive model selection. The third is extending RA from reproduction to autonomous algorithm discovery. The authors state that RA outperforms several more expensive models at lower cost, but that fully reliable reproduction at greater efficiency remains an open challenge.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Reliable reproduction depends on consistent records, and the authors propose extending the approach to other fields and algorithm discovery.

sections.body:
SI A gives background for the reproduction tasks. It defines classical simulation of observable expectation values and reviews six method classes: tensor networks, neural quantum states, Pauli propagation, quantum Monte Carlo methods, Lindbladian simulation and free-fermion simulation. For each class it gives the formulation, the computational principles and the conditions for efficient simulation. The section also covers quantum algorithms, quantum-property characterization, representative agents and harnesses, and related work on AI scientists in computational quantum science.

The visible text also contains case studies of RA repairs. In one, a noisy-regime cost estimate was corrected after the critic found that the circuit schedules violated a stated bound on the power-law exponent. In another, the critic used probing agents on small experiments, and majority voting selected the fixes that restored the reported curves for Paper #29.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix reviews classical simulation, quantum algorithms, property characterization, agent harnesses and related AI scientist work.
